items.title: Thaler's 2017 Nobel marked behavioural economics' mainstreaming
items.claim: Richard Thaler won the 2017 Nobel for contributions to behavioural economics. What's a flagship policy application of his work?

options.text: Save More Tomorrow (SMarT) — pension auto-escalation programmes where employees commit in advance to allocate future salary increases to savings. Adoption rates and savings rates rose substantially in trials

items.reveal:
Thaler and Benartzi's SMarT (2004) is one of the most replicated behavioural interventions. Auto-enrolment to UK workplace pensions (Pensions Act 2008, rolled out 2012-18) raised pension participation from ~55% to ~90%.

The UK's Behavioural Insights Team ('Nudge Unit') was set up in 2010, partly privatised in 2014, now operates internationally. Sunstein worked in the Obama administration on regulatory nudges.

Critics (Gerd Gigerenzer) argue some 'biases' are adaptive heuristics; defenders point to robust effects in field experiments.
items.why: Behavioural economics has moved from contested research programme to standard policy toolkit in two decades. The implementation often outruns settled debates about which biases are 'real' vs adaptive.

items.title: The UK's 2010-2015 austerity programme
items.claim: The UK government under Osborne (2010-2016) pursued fiscal consolidation. What was the actual deficit reduction trajectory?

options.text: Budget deficit fell from ~10% of GDP (2009-10) to ~4% by 2015-16, but the target of eliminating it by 2015 was missed; growth was slower than OBR projections; public investment was cut sharply

items.reveal:
ONS data: UK fiscal deficit was 10.1% of GDP in 2009-10, 4.1% by 2015-16. The original 2010 emergency budget aimed to balance the structural deficit by 2015; the target was slipped repeatedly.

IFS and OBR analyses found growth fell short of pre-austerity forecasts. Economic historians (Blyth 'Austerity', 2013) and IMF research raised doubts about the timing of consolidation; defenders (Niemietz, others) argued the policy preserved fiscal credibility.

The austerity debate continues; the empirical record is contested but the speed of recovery was slower than baseline.
items.why: Major macroeconomic policy choices have decade-long effects that are hard to evaluate cleanly because counterfactuals are unobservable.

items.title: The Bank of England became independent in 1997
items.claim: Gordon Brown announced operational independence for the Bank of England in May 1997, days after Labour's election victory. What's the standard rationale?

options.text: To allow politicians to set interest rates directly

To insulate monetary policy from short-term political pressure, given evidence that independent central banks (Bundesbank, Fed) had lower average inflation. The Treasury sets the target; the Bank sets rates

items.reveal:
Alesina and Summers (1993) had documented the inverse correlation between central bank independence and inflation across OECD countries. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's 1989 Act pioneered explicit inflation targeting.

UK target: 2% CPI from 2003 (RPIX 2.5% before). The MPC has 9 members, votes monthly. Brown's surprise announcement preceded the post-1997 inflation stability period.

Independence has been challenged in some quarters since 2010s rate decisions; the Bank's bond buying in autumn 2022 (LDI crisis) raised questions about coordination with Treasury.
items.why: Institutional design — who decides what, accountable to whom — is as much a part of macroeconomic policy as the decisions themselves.
